record.title: Learned classical energies report large efficiency gains on structured reasoning puzzles
record.summary: A Nov 12 preprint introduces Compact Reasoning Associative Memory (CRAM), a learned pairwise-energy model that solves structured constraint puzzles through recurrent energy descent. The authors report three-seed test results on Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Unique, N-Queens and graph coloring; the abstract reports 99.996% Sudoku-Extreme and 100% Maze-Unique accuracy after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one H200, respectively. The paper reports at least 1,000× faster fitting than the compared looped models on these tasks and at least 282× fewer Sudoku inference FLOPs at matched baseline accuracy. These are author-reported results on structured puzzle families, not evidence of comparable performance on open-ended reasoning.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The authors posted arXiv:2611.17309v1 on November 12, 2026, describing a learned energy model called Compact Reasoning Associative Memory (CRAM).

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report three-seed Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Unique, N-Queens and graph-coloring experiments; the abstract reports 99.996% Sudoku-Extreme and 100% Maze-Unique test accuracy, with 42 ms and 132 ms training times on one H200, and at least 1,000× faster fitting than compared looped models.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors report at least 282× fewer Sudoku inference FLOPs than looped baselines at matched baseline accuracy; their comparison includes all search chains and failed searches.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The inspected paper does not establish comparable performance on open-ended reasoning or tasks requiring inferred latent quantities; the authors caution that high accuracy on these structured puzzles does not show scalability to harder tasks.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent matched reproduction of the reported training, accuracy or inference-FLOP comparisons was inspected.
The paper does not establish transfer beyond structured constraint puzzles to open-ended tasks requiring inferred latent quantities.

brief.importance_rationale: If true in the stated structured-puzzle regime, this changes local architecture and benchmark choices by showing that a learned pairwise-energy system can report very large training and inference-compute reductions on several constraint tasks. The authors explicitly caution that these results do not establish open-ended reasoning scalability.
limitations: All performance numbers are reported by the paper authors and were not independently reproduced in this review.
The experiments concern structured constraint-puzzle families; the authors state this does not establish scaling to harder open-ended reasoning tasks.
Fit-time comparisons use different process protocols: baseline runs in fresh processes, while CRAM is reported as a median of seven runs after a first run in the same process.
No code or artifact audit was performed in this activation.
brief.summary: A Nov 12 preprint introduces Compact Reasoning Associative Memory (CRAM), a learned pairwise-energy model that solves structured constraint puzzles through recurrent energy descent. The authors report three-seed test results on Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Unique, N-Queens and graph coloring; the abstract reports 99.996% Sudoku-Extreme and 100% Maze-Unique accuracy after 42 ms and 132 ms of training on one H200, respectively. The paper reports at least 1,000× faster fitting than the compared looped models on these tasks and at least 282× fewer Sudoku inference FLOPs at matched baseline accuracy. These are author-reported results on structured puzzle families, not evidence of comparable performance on open-ended reasoning.

technical.claimed_result: Authors report 99.996% Sudoku-Extreme and 100% Maze-Unique accuracy, 42 ms/132 ms fit times on one H200, at least 1,000× faster fit than compared looped models, and at least 282× fewer Sudoku inference FLOPs at matched baseline accuracy.
technical.compute_or_cost: The paper reports fitting in 42 ms on Sudoku-Extreme and 132 ms on Maze-Unique on one H200; reported training-time comparison is author-run and uses different process protocols.
technical.demonstrated_result: The preprint is accessible and reports a three-seed experimental design and explicit timing/FLOP protocols. This review did not independently reproduce the outcomes.
technical.mechanism: CRAM learns symmetric pairwise costs and biases over puzzle variables, then uses recurrent energy descent and focused Gibbs search to find low-energy assignments; a fitted energy threshold can stop search early.
technical.novelty: Learns an explicit classical pairwise energy from solved puzzles and uses it as both the learned representation and inference objective; emphasizes the narrowness of puzzle benchmarks as a proxy for general reasoning.
technical.regime: Structured Sudoku-Extreme, Maze-Unique, N-Queens and graph-coloring tasks with task-specific variable structures and priors; experiments reported on one H200.
technical.reproducibility: No independent reproduction or code audit performed in this activation; the paper links research artifacts but they were not inspected.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares with seven looped-model implementations, including HRM, TRM, GRAM, EqR, FRM, TRMP and EBR. It reports three-seed means for most baselines and notes published scores where its reproduction was lower. Fit-time process protocol differs between baselines and CRAM.

brief.title: Learned classical energies report large efficiency gains on structured reasoning puzzles
brief.why_it_matters: If the reported comparisons hold in their stated regime, learned pairwise energies offer a much smaller and faster alternative to deep looped models for some constraint problems. The work also warns that near-perfect scores on simple, rule-structured puzzles may say little about scaling to tasks requiring latent-variable inference; both points can affect architecture choices and benchmark design.
